newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon 1996 economic growth slows to four percent.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon 1996 economic growth slows to four percent.

text.p: Lebanon's economic growth slipped to four percent in 1996 from 6.5 percent in 1995, well below the 10 percent growth rate projected in the government's postwar reconstruction programme, a leading bank said on Wednesday.

"The economic growth rate recorded in 1996, four percent, remained far lower than its targeted level in the reconstruction plan, 10 percent," Fransabank said in its fourth quarter report on the economy.

One reason for the slowdown was that much of the reconstruction spending was going abroad in import payments -- which exceeded $7 billion in 1996 -- and payments to foreign workers and foreign firms involved in reconstruction, it said.

Other factors were "the stagnated world economy, Israeli aggression on Lebanon in April, weak aggregate supply and shrinking growth in aggregate demand, and the faster growth in government deficit and debt," Fransabank added.
The cost of the 17-day Israeli blitz that killed 200 people and forced 400,000 refugees to flee south Lebanon is estimated at $300-$500 million, or 2.3-3.8 percent of GDP, the bank said.
It said that according to ministry of finance estimates, the 1996 growth rate raised Lebanon's real GDP to nearly $13.2 billion from $11.3 billion a year earlier.
"With our estimated figures for private transfers, the nation's real GNP is estimated to run at almost $14.2 billion in 1996 against $12.1 billion in 1995," the bank said.
Per capita GDP rose to $3,485 per year, it added.

It said during the first phase of the reconstruction plan (1993-1996), the government had secured monetary stability, relative price stability and high growth rates and had attracted foreign capital and recorded big balance of payments surpluses.
It had also rehabilitated much of the country's infrastructure and had improved investment conditions and enlarged the Beirut financial markets.

Despite the dip in economic growth in 1996, Lebanon had put itself back on the list of interesting emerging markets during the year "as the government and several banks achieved a major success in entering international financial markets via substantial financial issues," Fransabank said.

It said the banking sector had historic success in 1996, through equity and debt issues raising hundreds of millions of dollars on international markets, a rise of 31.5 percent in assets and a 32.1 percent increase in deposits.

"The positive record of economic achievements during the past four years has convinced foreign parties of the ability of the Lebanese economic administration to run growth in spite of the unfavourable regional and international changes," it said.
Despite a trade balance deficit of $6.4 billion in 1996, compared with $5.7 billion in 1995, the balance of payments surplus tripled to $780 million from increasing capital inflows, Fransabank added.

But on a negative note, net public debt rose 45.5 percent to $10.3 billion in 1996, compared with a 47.3 percent in 1995, due to the growth of the budget deficit and a big increase in interest payments on public borrowing, it said.

"Relative to GDP, net public debt galloped from 63 percent in 1995 to nearly 78.2 percent in 1996. Also the ratio of public debt to the country's level of international reserves jumped from 88.2 percent to 111.3 percent.
"These figures clearly underline the seriousness of the fiscal problem. The government expects the debt/GDP ratio to reach 82.2 percent in 1997," the bank added.
